## Three questions

::: {.smaller}
1. **Can a responder act on a single flagged building?**
2. **Do they at least rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage?**
3. **What is the sensible way to use them** in the next event?
:::

::: {.tiny}
M7.5, coastal Venezuela, 24 June 2026. At least 8 organisations released damage products; we
evaluated the 6 that published an analysed extent. Numbers frozen to the 2026-07-15 snapshot.
:::

## Performance metrics by model

![](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_best_f1_r10_slides.png){.r-stretch}

## Can they rank the worst-hit neighbourhoods?

![](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3f_null_ranking_both_slides.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway style="font-size:0.66em"}
Yes: products can support neighbourhood-level prioritisation. In the core region every
product ranks the worst-hit cells far better than chance (ρ 0.48–0.74, n = 133 cells,
all p < 10⁻⁸). As delivered the correlations are much lower (−0.09 to 0.58), and UH is
statistically indistinguishable from zero.
:::

## Precision & recall: single products vs combinations

![](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5b_frontier_r10.png){.r-stretch}

## Three questions, three answers

::: {.smaller}
1. **Can a responder act on a single flagged building?** **No.** Precision runs
   0.05–0.09 even in the damage-dense core region: most flags have nothing wrong
   underneath them.
2. **Do they rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage?** **Yes, with a condition.**
   Where the damage zone is known and confined (our core region), most products show
   real prioritisation value (ρ 0.48–0.74); as delivered the signal is much weaker
   (ρ −0.09 to 0.58).
3. **What is the sensible way to use them in the next event?** **Still open.** The
   promising lines:
   - **Combine products.** Counting agreement between independent products roughly
     doubled the accuracy of the best single one here, with no reference data needed.
   - **Match the operating point to the moment.** Different stages of a response may
     favour precision or coverage differently; field and first-responder feedback
     should establish where and when higher precision beats broader coverage (open).
   - **Improve the models.** Evaluations like this one show providers where the
     failures are.
:::

## We scored against three references, not one

![](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/reference_architecture.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway}
Expert damage points from Copernicus EMS, crowd review of AI flags via MapSwipe, and 415
reports from teams on the ground. Each is blind to something the others can see, which lets us
turn them on **each other** as well as on the products.
:::

## The reference has its own blind spot

::: {.cols}
::: {.col}
Copernicus EMS captured:

::: {.bignum}
94%
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
of field-reported **destroyed** buildings
:::

::: {.bignum}
49%
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
of field-reported **damaged** buildings
:::
:::
::: {.col}
![](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png)
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
So the expert map is thorough about destruction and patchy about everything short of it.
Any precision scored against it is therefore a **floor**: Microsoft's climbs from 0.08 to
roughly 0.24 once the crowd confirms damage that CEMS never recorded.
:::

## What "right" and "wrong" mean here {.smaller}

::: {.cols}
::: {.col style="flex:1.35"}
![](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_dual_anchor_matching.png)
:::
::: {.col}
A few streets in Caraballeda, Microsoft against the expert map.

- **Green**: a flagged building with expert-recorded damage within 10 m. A hit.
- **Orange**: a flagged building with nothing recorded near it.
- **Black dots**: expert damage points the product caught.
- **Red circles**: expert damage points it missed. There are a lot of them.

::: {.takeaway}
**Precision** asks what share of the coloured footprints are green. **Recall** asks what share
of the points are black rather than red. Neither needs a count of the grey buildings, which is
why "how many did it get right out of everything" is the wrong question.
:::
:::
:::

## The benchmark we measured against

![](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_dayzero_schematic.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway-hot}
Three things you know within hours of any earthquake: how far a building sits from the coast,
how densely built its neighbourhood is, and how hard the ground shook. Fitting them into a model
does require the damage map itself, so read the red caveat: this is a **yardstick we can only
hold up afterwards**, not a tool anyone had on the day.
:::

## Zoom out, though, and they do a decent job

![](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_priority_map.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.takeaway}
Stop asking about individual buildings and ask which *neighbourhoods* to go to first, and the
picture improves a lot. Microsoft and OSU each pick 6 of the 10 worst-hit sectors, and rank
correlation with the expert damage count runs about 0.54–0.59. This is the scale at which the
products are genuinely useful.
:::

## What actually works: their disagreement

::: {.smaller}
| rule | flags | precision floor | crowd-adjusted | damage coverage | visits per find |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| any of 6 | 37,644 | 0.03 | 0.21 | 0.97 | 26.4 |
| 3 of 6 | 9,409 | 0.10 | 0.28 | 0.86 | 7.5 |
| **4 of 6** | **3,347** | **0.19** | **0.38** | **0.67** | **3.4** |
| all 6 | 214 | 0.64 | 0.93 | 0.18 | 0.8 |
:::

::: {.takeaway}
The products fail in **different** places, so the number of them agreeing on a building tells
you how much to believe it. That gives you a dial with a known price at every setting: choose
by how many teams you have and how much a wasted trip costs you.
:::

## The one finding to take into the next event

::: {.hero}
2×
:::
::: {.hero-sub}
Counting agreement **between independent products** roughly doubles the accuracy of any
single one
:::

::: {.smaller}
- It needs **no weights, no training data, no reference**; it is computable the hour the second
  product lands.
- A learned fusion scores 18% higher, **but its weights come from the damage map you are still
  waiting for.** Like the geography yardstick, it explains an event afterwards; it cannot run
  during one.
:::

::: {.takeaway-hot}
**It is the only method we tested that is both effective and available on day one.**
:::

## Three honest caveats on that

::: {.smaller}
1. **"Flat" means equal trust.** UH, with as-delivered precision 0.009, casts a full vote. That
   it *helped* is real, but we could only establish that with a reference in hand.
2. **Count independent methods, not raw products.** Five products sharing one method would
   inherit its bias no matter how many agreed; here the two coherence products already
   agree for the wrong reason. Independence is what mattered, not the modality label: the
   best pair was two optical products with nothing else in common.
3. **Choosing *k* buys a workload, not a hit rate.** Flag counts are observable without labels;
   the precision they deliver is not.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
None of this changes the advice. It does change how carefully we should phrase it.
:::

## Why one product's failure could be diagnosed

![](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_west_cluster_adjudication.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.smaller}
Top left: where Microsoft flags far more damage than the expert map records. Bottom left: where
volunteers said there was nothing there. Across the **western strip as a whole**, reviewers
judged **71%** of Microsoft's flags undamaged, against a roughly even split in the damage-dense
east. Right: cell by cell the two do *not* track ($\rho$ = +0.09); the agreement is at the
scale of the strip, not the individual hex. That strip sat under a **single satellite scene**,
processed on its own with no cross-scene check. Cross-check: **UH ran on the same imagery
vendor** over the same strip and flags just 3% there (Microsoft: 32%), so the failure travelled
with the model, not the pixels.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Microsoft was alone in publishing **per-building acquisition metadata**, and that is exactly
why it is the only product whose biggest failure we could explain instead of merely notice. The
others may well have similar problems. We simply have no way to look.
:::

## What we would ask for

::: {.smaller}
**Responders**: do not spend time choosing a product; spend it counting agreement between
independent products. Use area rankings for triage. Nothing here sees light damage reliably.

**Providers**: publish an analysed extent (without one a product cannot be evaluated at all),
publish per-building acquisition metadata, and validate where you deploy rather than where
validation data happens to exist. The failing scene here was the unvalidated one.

**Evaluators**: publish precision as a lower bound, or adjudicate against a second reference
and publish the interval. Check new products against a geography-only yardstick.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
And close the coverage gap: inland communities missed by **every** product were inside analysed
extents, and nobody knew nobody was looking.
:::

## Where this is weakest

::: {.smaller}
- **One event, one coastal urban geography.** 96% of the reference sits in one coastal strip
  (Caraballeda), so pooled numbers are effectively that strip's numbers.
- **The geography yardstick is fitted on this event's labels**: an information-content claim,
  not an operational one. A model trained on *previous* earthquakes is the honest next step and
  is untested.
- **Confidence intervals are wide.** Resampling whole neighbourhoods moves single-product
  numbers a lot: no single product separates from the geography yardstick, while the
  combination rules clear it decisively. The accuracy-versus-arrival-date analysis is pending.
- Rankings and orderings are robust; absolute magnitudes inherit a thin reference.
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Treat this as one carefully worked case and a method you can re-run, rather than a verdict on
these products in general.
:::

## Appendix · how the crowd adjustment works, and its independent re-test

![](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_crowd_adjustment_explainer.png){.r-stretch}

::: {.tiny}
Every "crowd-adjusted" number in this deck is this mechanism: an unmatched flag is adjudicated
by its ~50 m crowd cell, and a majority-"Yes" cell adds it back to the precision numerator. In
Jul–Aug 2026 an independent crowd re-voted the same 3,482 cells at 3× the vote depth: individual
cells flip (purple), but the share of flags confirmed barely moves, from **13.2%** to **11.5%**, so the
adjusted numbers hold as (mildly generous) upper estimates. Round 2 offered no "No damage"
answer, so round 1's 71%-said-No statistic is not re-testable; the confirmation side is what
replicates.
:::
